sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: The Rematch
case.hook: Uh oh. Coach Dee runs the Dune Hill derby team, and she just texted me about my hay bale plan.

thread.t: Sam! Your hay plan is WRONG. I tested it myself this morning. 😤
Light car from the HIGH ramp: 15 inches. Heavy car from the LOW ramp: 16 inches. Same push! Height doesn’t matter.
Hmm. Was it the same car both times?
No, the heavy one has the new wheels. Oh, and it got windy.
One try each. That’s proof, right? 🏁
Let’s run a FAIR test. I’ll send you the results.

case.question: Does the start height really matter? How can Sam prove it to Coach Dee?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: You timed the same car 3 times and got 3 different times. Small differences are normal, so one try can fool you.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: lock it down
clues.t: Coach Dee changed 4 things at once. When ONLY the start height changed, the High start pushed 25 inches and the Low start only 8.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: dot plot drop
clues.t: Many trials pile up around a typical number. The middle of the pile is easier to trust than any one try.
One odd trial was caused by a sock on the track. Checking and redoing it kept the test honest: Low 8, Middle 16, High 25 inches.

solve.title: How can Sam prove it?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Coach Dee is right. Her test proves start height doesn’t matter.
options.why: Check Clue 2. How many things changed in her test?

options.t: One more try from each ramp will settle it.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 3. Can one try be trusted?

options.t: Run a fair test: same car, same wheels, same weather, and change ONLY the start height. Do several trials. The High start pushes farthest, so the hay plan stays.
options.why: Case cracked! A fair test with many trials shows the High start really does push the hay the farthest. Coach Dee agrees, and she wants a rematch. Bullseye Derby is open, just below!

options.t: Throw out any numbers that don’t match the plan.
options.why: Check Clue 4. What should you do with an odd number?

stopwatch.title: The stopwatch race
todo: Press Start when the car passes the green flag. Press Stop at the red flag.
Do it 3 times. Do your times match?

why.t: Distance ÷ time = speed. To know how fast the car goes, you need a good time.

stopwatch.alt: A model: a derby car rolls along a flat track past a green START flag and a red STOP flag.
stopwatch.realLine: The car takes exactly the same time every run. Your times are a little different because people press a little early or a little late.
stopwatch.missLine: The car got away! Roll it again. Press Start at the green flag and Stop at the red flag.
stopwatch.early: That was early! The car hadn’t reached the green flag. It still counts. Real scientists make small timing mistakes too.

opts.t: People press a little early or late, so every try is a little different.
The car changed speed every time.
opts.miss: Read the laser timer. Was the car’s real time the same every run?

opts.t: I did something wrong, so I should throw those times out.
opts.miss: Small differences are normal in every test. That’s why scientists do several trials, not why they throw them out.

stopwatch.win: Same car, same flags, three different times. That’s why scientists never trust just one try. Clue 1!

lockdown.title: Lock it down
todo: Red rows changed between her two runs. Click 🔓 to keep a row the same.
Lock everything except the ONE thing we test. Then run the fair test.

why.t: Anything that could change in a test. A fair test changes only ONE variable and keeps all the others the same.

lockdown.testMiss: If both cars start at the same height, what would you be testing? Keep the start ramps different. Lock the OTHER rows.

deeResult.t: About the same push. But the car, the wheels and the wind changed too. Which one made the difference? Nobody can tell!

fairResult.t: Now ONLY the start height changed. The High start pushed 25 inches. The Low start pushed 8. The height made the difference.

lockdown.q: Why couldn’t Coach Dee trust her test?

opts.t: She changed lots of things at once, so she can’t tell which one caused the result.

opts.miss: The hay bale stayed the same in both runs. Look at the red rows.
Speed isn’t the problem. How many rows were different between her two runs?

lockdown.win: Change ONE thing, keep the rest the same. That’s a fair test! Clue 2!

dotplot.title: Dot plot drop
todo: Press Run a trial. Each trial drops a dot (Middle start, how far the bale slid).
Drag the gold marker to the middle of the dots (or tap the number line).

why.t: A number line with one dot for each result. Where the dots pile up shows the typical result.

dotplot.alt: A number line from 0 to 30 inches with a dot for each trial and a gold marker.
dotplot.startLine: Run the first trial. One dot can’t tell you much yet.

trust.head: 1 trial
trust.t: Just one dot. Was it a normal run or a lucky one? You can’t tell yet.

trust.head: 3 trials
trust.t: A pile is starting to form. Keep going.

trust.head: 5 trials
trust.t: Now there’s a clear pile. Drag the gold marker to its middle.

trust.head: 7 trials
trust.t: More trials, same pile. Now you can really trust the middle.

dotplot.moreLine: Run at least {n} trials first. One or two dots can fool you.
dotplot.lowLine: More dots are to the right of your marker. Slide it toward the middle of the pile.
dotplot.highLine: More dots are to the left of your marker. Slide it toward the middle of the pile.

opts.t: The dots pile up around a typical number, so one odd try can’t fool you.
More trials make the car go faster.
opts.miss: The car is the same every trial. What does the pile of dots show you?

opts.t: Five is the rule for every test.
opts.miss: There’s no magic number. What happens to the pile as you add dots?

dotplot.win: The middle of the pile is about 16 inches. Many trials show the pattern. Clue 3!

bulletin.title: Coach Dee’s voicemail
todo: Press Play and listen. You can read along.
Tap the 3 things that made her test UNFAIR.
lines: Sam, it’s Coach Dee. I tested your hay plan myself!
I sent the [[cars|light car down the High ramp and the heavy car]] down [[x:The start ramp is the ONE thing she is testing. Changing it is OK! Look for something else that changed.|the Low ramp]].
Oh, and it got [[wind|really windy]] right after the first run.
They pushed the bale about the same, so height doesn’t matter. I only needed [[once|one try each]]. Call me back!

dangers.does: a light car and a heavy car with new wheels
windy for only one of the runs
one try can be a fluke

bulletin.win: Three problems in one test! No wonder the results were confusing.

detective.title: Data detective
todo: Read Coach Dee’s notebook. Tap the number that doesn’t fit.
Decide what to do with it.

why.t: A result that is way off because of an accident, not because of the thing you are testing.

detective.head: Coach Dee’s Fair Test · Dune Hill
detective.sub: Same car, same wheels, calm air. Only the start changes. How far the hay bale slid:
detective.note: Trial 3 from the Middle was weird. I was busy hanging my lucky socks on the fence to dry… (Dee)
detective.fitLine: That number fits with the others in its row. Look for one that is way off.
detective.choiceQ: You found it! What should a scientist do with this odd number?

choices.miss: If something went wrong in that run, it isn’t telling you about the start height. Find out first.

choices.t: Throw it out. It doesn’t match.
choices.miss: Throwing out a number just because you don’t like it isn’t fair. First find out WHY it’s odd.

choices.t: Check what happened, then redo that trial.

replay.head: Replay of the odd trial
replay.alt: A replay: the derby car rolls down the hill and stops short when it hits a sock lying on the track.
replay.cap: A sock blew off the fence onto the track! The car hit it and stopped early. The odd number came from an accident, not from the start height.

detective.avgLabel: Averages: the typical push from each start (inches)

opts.t: The higher the start, the farther the push: about 8, 16 and 25 inches.

opts.miss: Compare the three bars. Are they the same height?

opts.t: The Middle start was weird, so the test failed.
opts.miss: The weird number had a cause, and you redid it. Read the bars now.

detective.win: Caught the fluke, checked it and redid it. Now the pattern is clear. Clue 4!

bullseye.title: Bullseye Derby
todo: Pick a start height with the slider.
Press Let it roll. Try to stop right on the bullseye!
Beat all 3 levels. Can you get 9 stars?

why.t: A higher start means more speed and more energy, so the car rolls farther before rubbing stops it.

bullseye.alt: A model: a hill on the left, a flat track with distance marks and a red and white bullseye target.

levels.name: Smooth pavement
levels.tip0: Level 1: smooth pavement. Pick a height and let it roll!
levels.tip: Higher start, more energy, longer roll.

levels.name: Smooth pavement, far target
levels.tip0: Level 2: the bullseye moved farther away. More height, or less?

levels.name: Bumpy sand
levels.tip0: Level 3: SAND! Sand rubs the wheels more, so the car stops sooner. Adjust your height!
levels.tip: Sand takes the energy away faster.

bullseye.lockLine: Crack the case first. Then Bullseye Derby opens.

lines.short: Too slow! Not enough energy to reach the target. Start higher.
lines.long: Too fast! Too much energy, and it blasted past the target. Start lower.
lines.done: You beat every level, derby champion!

q1.A: Not that kind of trial! In science, what is one run of a test called?
q1.C: A measurement is a number you get. What do we call one run of the test?

q2.B: Where it happens doesn’t make it fair. Think about Lock it down.
q2.C: Scientists don’t control the result. What did you lock in Lock it down?

q3.A: Changing the marble changes two things! Which change controls speed?
q3.B: The target should stay the same. Which change controls the marble’s speed?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-2: Think about your 3 stopwatch times. Did they match?
Think about the dot plot. What did the pile of dots show?
Try: Scientists run more than one trial because ___. Many trials show a pattern, like ___.
ans-3: Think about Coach Dee’s test in Lock it down.
If two things changed, could you tell which one caused the result?
Try: They can’t trust it because ___. A controlled test ___.
cer-4: First decide: is one roll enough?
Think about your stopwatch times and Coach Dee’s sock.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

welcome.label: Welcome · the rematch
welcome.script: Uh oh. Coach Dee texted me. She tested my hay plan once, and she says start height doesn’t matter! Read our text messages. Is her test fair? Let’s find out, the scientist way.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · the stopwatch race (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Can you time a race perfectly? Press Roll the car. Press Start at the green flag and Stop at the red flag. Do it three times. Do your three times match?

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Use a real stopwatch or phone timer for “time”; a ruler for “distance” and “measurement”.

part1.label: Part 1 · lock it down (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s Coach Dee’s test on my control panel. The red rows changed between her two runs. Click the padlocks to keep them the same. Lock everything except the start height. Then run both tests.

part2.label: Part 2 · dot plot drop (Clue 3)
part2.script: Time for lots of trials! Press Run a trial, again and again. Watch the dots pile up. Then drag the gold marker to the middle of the pile.

explore.label: Part 4 · data detective (Clue 4)
explore.script: Coach Dee ran nine trials after all! Look at her notebook. One number looks really strange. Tap it. Then decide: keep it, throw it out, or check and redo?

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab. Then answer two questions, fill in your nine trial table, and finish your C-E-R. And after the case, a bonus game opens!

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says one roll down a ramp is a whole investigation. Hmm. Think about your stopwatch times and Coach Dee’s sock. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Coach Dee says the hay plan stays, and she challenged you to Bullseye Derby! Next week, we follow the energy. How does it move from one place to another?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain what makes evidence trustworthy?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “fair test”, “only one thing” and “the same”. Those words hold the big idea. Small words like “a” and “and” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
